title: India Is About to Pay Companies to Process Lithium and Nickel. The Minimum Entry Is 30,000 Tonnes.
excerpt: A ₹3,000 crore incentive package for critical mineral processing is imminent, targeting the chokehold China has on India's EV battery supply chain.
body:
India's Ministry of Mines is on the verge of unveiling an incentive policy worth approximately ₹3,000 crore ($313 million) to kickstart domestic processing of lithium and nickel, according to sources familiar with the plan. The move is aimed squarely at breaking China's stranglehold on the critical minerals that power every electric vehicle battery India hopes to build.

The policy has been months in the making. Reuters first reported in January that the incentive scheme would cover lithium and nickel. In April, the mines secretary confirmed that two critical minerals linked to "securing an electric vehicle value system" had been shortlisted. Now, the formal rollout is imminent.

## The Terms

The incentive plan proposes a 15 per cent capital subsidy for eligible investments in lithium and nickel processing projects starting on or after April 1, 2026. But the barriers to entry are deliberately high. Lithium processing plants must have a minimum capacity of 30,000 metric tonnes. Nickel plants must hit at least 50,000 tonnes.

The subsidy is capped at 40 per cent of annual net sales turnover for lithium operations and 25 per cent for nickel, disbursed in stages tied to minimum plant utilisation targets. Incentives will be available for five years.

The government initially plans to seed the programme with two lithium and two nickel projects — just enough to meet the country's projected domestic demand by 2030.

## Why It Matters

The numbers tell the story. India targets 30 per cent electric car penetration and 80 per cent for two-wheelers by 2030. Today, those figures stand at six per cent and nine per cent respectively. Every one of those vehicles needs a lithium-ion battery. And right now, China processes roughly 65 per cent of the world's lithium and 35 per cent of its nickel into battery-grade material.

India has some domestic lithium reserves — geological surveys in Jammu and Kashmir's Reasi district identified 5.9 million tonnes of lithium ore in 2023, the country's first significant find. But ore is not the same as processed, battery-grade lithium carbonate or hydroxide. Without processing capacity, the discovery is a geological curiosity, not a strategic asset.

The same logic applies to nickel. India's nickel consumption has risen sharply alongside its stainless steel and battery industries, but it imports nearly all of its refined nickel. Indonesia, the world's largest nickel producer, has already imposed export bans on raw ore to force downstream processing at home. India does not want to be on the receiving end of that supply-chain leverage.

## The Bigger Picture

The lithium-nickel programme sits within a broader critical minerals strategy that has accelerated markedly over the past two years. In the 2026–27 Union Budget, the government announced Dedicated Rare Earth Corridors and a ₹7,280 crore scheme for rare earth permanent magnet manufacturing. KABIL, the government's critical minerals acquisition arm, has signed agreements with Argentina for lithium brine exploration. India joined the US-led Minerals Security Partnership in 2023, aligning itself with Western supply-chain diversification efforts.

The geopolitical context adds urgency. The Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz have exposed how quickly energy supply chains can be disrupted. Critical minerals — which travel similar trade routes — face the same vulnerabilities. Building domestic processing capacity is not just an industrial policy. It is an insurance policy.

## The Challenge

A 15 per cent capital subsidy, however generous on paper, still requires companies to commit billions in upfront investment for plants that will take years to reach full utilisation. India's track record on large-scale industrial incentive schemes is mixed — the Production Linked Incentive programme for electronics has produced results; similar schemes in other sectors have moved slowly.

The minimum capacity thresholds are also a double-edged sword. They ensure scale, but they rule out smaller, more agile players who might move faster. And the five-year incentive window is tight for projects of this complexity.

Still, the direction of travel is unmistakable. India cannot build an EV economy on imported batteries. This is the first serious attempt to make sure it does not have to.

*Sources: Reuters, The Hindu BusinessLine, Engineering News, Press Information Bureau*
